# Executive summary

**Note:** This is a work in progress and will be updated regularly.

# Data

The [SMARD API](https://smard.api.bund.dev/) of the German Federal Network Agency provides easy access to different energy-related time series for Germany at various observation frequencies. In this project, we will focus on forecasting an entire week (in 15-minute intervals) of the overall energy consumption in Germany using data observed with a frequency of 15 minutes. To access the data, it is recommended to use my Python extension [`smardapi`](https://github.com/dschulz13/smardapi_python), which can be easily installed from GitHub using `pip install git+https://github.com/dschulz13/smardapi_python.git` in the terminal.

<details><summary>Show Python code for downloading the data</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: True
#| eval: False
#| include: True

import smardapi as api
import gc

print(api.allowed_filter_no())
print(api.allowed_region())
print(api.allowed_resolution())

api.specify(filter_no = 410, region = 'DE')
api.download(resolution = 'quarterhour', start = '2015-01-01', stop = '2026-11-08 23:59:00')

api.data.to_feather('German_Energy_Consumption_20150101_to_20261108.feather')

del(api)
gc.collect()
```

</details>

A first overview of the data is obtained by inspecting the following 3D-figure @fig-threeD. Since Germany has winter and summer times, where in spring the clock once jumps from 02:00 AM to 03:00 AM and in fall it goes back once from 03:00 AM to 02:00 AM, a representation in German time is difficult. Therefore, for the missing times 02:00 AM, 02:15 AM, 02:30 AM, and 02:45 AM on one day each year in spring, we fill these values up for @fig-threeD by linear interpolation between the observed values at 01:45 AM and 03:00 AM. In contrast, in fall we have two sets of values during one night at 02:00 AM, 02:15 AM, 02:30 AM, and 02:45 AM. In these cases, we construct the arithmetic mean of the two available observations at each time point and consider those for @fig-threeD.

<details><summary>Show Python code for the 3D graphic</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: True
#| eval: False

# Imports
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Construct the decimal year from an array with string dates
def to_decimal_year(x):
    year_start = pd.to_datetime(pd.to_datetime(x).dt.year.astype(str) + '-01-01')
    next_year_start = pd.to_datetime((pd.to_datetime(x).dt.year + 1).astype(str) + '-01-01')
    tp_date = pd.to_datetime(x)
    return (tp_date - year_start) / (next_year_start - year_start) + tp_date.dt.year

# Read in the data
dataset = pd.read_feather('German_Energy_Consumption_20150101_to_20261108.feather')
df_plot = dataset.copy()
dims = dataset.shape

# Time of day variable (in decimal time)
df_plot['tof'] = dataset['Timestamp'].dt.hour + dataset['Timestamp'].dt.minute / 60
# Decimal year variable
df_plot['dec_year'] = to_decimal_year(dataset['Timestamp'].dt.date)
# Drop timestamp variable
df_plot = df_plot.drop(['Timestamp'], axis = 1)


# Get time differences between sequential observations
df_plot['timediff'] = 0.25   # Default of a quarter of an hour
# Fill slots with actual time differences
df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'timediff'] = df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'tof'].to_numpy() - df_plot.loc[0:(dims[0] - 2), 'tof'].to_numpy()
# Jumps of -23.75 are when going from 11:45 PM to 00:00 AM and are
# also equivalent to a quarter-hour progression
df_plot.loc[df_plot['timediff'] == -23.75, 'timediff'] = 0.25
# Identify where the clock goes back an hour
backw_mask = df_plot['timediff'] == -0.75
idx_backw = backw_mask[backw_mask].index
# 
for i in reversed(range(0, idx_backw.shape[0])):
    idx = idx_backw[i]
    # Replace first set of values with averages
    df_plot.loc[(idx - 4):(idx - 1), 'Value'] = (df_plot.loc[idx:(idx + 3), 'Value'].to_numpy() + df_plot.loc[(idx - 4):(idx - 1), 'Value'].to_numpy()) / 2
    # Drop second set of values
    df_plot = df_plot.drop(range(idx, idx + 4), axis = 0)
        
# Reset the index
df_plot = df_plot.reset_index(drop = True)

dims = df_plot.shape

# Get again the time differences
df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'timediff'] = df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'tof'].to_numpy() - df_plot.loc[0:(dims[0] - 2), 'tof'].to_numpy()
df_plot.loc[df_plot['timediff'] == -23.75, 'timediff'] = 0.25
# Now identify the spots, where the clock jumps ahead
forw_mask = df_plot['timediff'] == 1.25
idx_forw = forw_mask[forw_mask].index
for i in range(0, idx_forw.shape[0]):
    # Set of missing times
    x = np.array([2.00, 2.25, 2.5, 2.75])
    # Available times at the boundaries
    xp = np.array([1.75, 3.00])
    # The observed series values at the available boundary points
    yp = np.array([df_plot.loc[idx_forw[i].item() - 1, 'Value'].item(), df_plot.loc[idx_forw[i].item(), 'Value'].item()])
    # Interpolate linearly
    val_interp = np.interp(x = x, xp = xp, fp = yp)
    # Add values to data frame
    df_add = pd.DataFrame({
        'Value': val_interp,
        'tof': x,
        'dec_year': df_plot.loc[idx_forw[i].item(), 'dec_year'].item(),
        'timediff': 0.25
    })
    df_plot = pd.concat([df_plot, df_add], axis = 0)

df_plot = (
    df_plot
        .drop(['timediff'], axis = 1)    # Drop timediff variable
        # Sort by day and time of day
        .sort_values(['dec_year', 'tof'], ascending = [True, True])
        # Reset the index
        .reset_index(drop = True)
)

# Number of available days
nday = len(df_plot.dec_year.unique())
# Number of available times
ntime = len(df_plot.tof.unique())
# Bring observed values into rectangular shape (and divide by 1000)
values = df_plot.Value.to_numpy().reshape(nday, ntime) / 1000
# Bring times into rectangular shape
tof = df_plot.tof.to_numpy().reshape(nday, ntime)
# Bring days into rectangular shape
date = df_plot.dec_year.to_numpy().reshape(nday, ntime)

# Construct surface plot (drop the scale)
fig = go.Figure(data = [go.Surface(z = values, x = date, y = tof, colorscale = "inferno", showscale = False)])

# Adjust title, labels, background color, etc.
fig.update_layout(
    title = 'Energy Consumption Germany',
    margin = dict(l = 20, r = 20, t = 30, b = 15),    
    scene = dict(
        aspectmode = "cube",
        xaxis = dict(
            title = "Decimal year",
            backgroundcolor = "white",
            gridcolor = "lightgrey",
            zerolinecolor = "lightgrey",
            autorange = "reversed"
        ),
        yaxis = dict(
            title = "Time of day",
            backgroundcolor = "white",
            gridcolor = "lightgrey",
            zerolinecolor = "lightgrey",
            autorange = "reversed"
        ),
        zaxis = dict(
            title = "GWh",
            backgroundcolor = "white",
            gridcolor = "lightgrey",
            zerolinecolor = "lightgrey"
        )
    ),
    paper_bgcolor = "white",
    plot_bgcolor = "white"
)
```

```{python}
def to_decimal_year(x):

    next_year_start = pd.to_datetime((pd.to_datetime(x).dt.year + 1).astype(str) + '-01-01')
    tp_date = pd.to_datetime(x)
    return (tp_date - year_start) / (next_year_start - year_start) + tp_date.dt.year

dataset = pd.read_feather('C:/Users/Dominik Schulz/Documents/Private Projects/energy_forecasting_python_project/German_Energy_Consumption_20150101_to_20261108.feather')
df_plot = dataset.copy()
dims = dataset.shape
df_plot['tof'] = dataset['Timestamp'].dt.hour + dataset['Timestamp'].dt.minute / 60
df_plot['dec_year'] = to_decimal_year(dataset['Timestamp'].dt.date)
df_plot = df_plot.drop(['Timestamp'], axis = 1)
df_plot['timediff'] = 0.25

df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'timediff'] = df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'tof'].to_numpy() - df_plot.loc[0:(dims[0] - 2), 'tof'].to_numpy()
df_plot.loc[df_plot['timediff'] == -23.75, 'timediff'] = 0.25
backw_mask = df_plot['timediff'] == -0.75
idx_backw = backw_mask[backw_mask].index
for i in reversed(range(0, idx_backw.shape[0])):
    idx = idx_backw[i]
    df_plot.loc[(idx - 4):(idx - 1), 'Value'] = (df_plot.loc[idx:(idx + 3), 'Value'].to_numpy() + df_plot.loc[(idx - 4):(idx - 1), 'Value'].to_numpy()) / 2
    df_plot = df_plot.drop(range(idx, idx + 4), axis = 0)
        
df_plot = df_plot.reset_index(drop = True)

dims = df_plot.shape
df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'timediff'] = df_plot.loc[1:(dims[0] - 1), 'tof'].to_numpy() - df_plot.loc[0:(dims[0] - 2), 'tof'].to_numpy()
df_plot.loc[df_plot['timediff'] == -23.75, 'timediff'] = 0.25
forw_mask = df_plot['timediff'] == 1.25
idx_forw = forw_mask[forw_mask].index
for i in range(0, idx_forw.shape[0]):
    x = np.array([2.00, 2.25, 2.5, 2.75])
    xp = np.array([1.75, 3.00])
    yp = np.array([df_plot.loc[idx_forw[i].item() - 1, 'Value'].item(), df_plot.loc[idx_forw[i].item(), 'Value'].item()])
    val_interp = np.interp(x = x, xp = xp, fp = yp)
    df_add = pd.DataFrame({
        'Value': val_interp,
        'tof': x,
        'dec_year': df_plot.loc[idx_forw[i].item(), 'dec_year'].item(),
        'timediff': 0.25
    })
    df_plot = pd.concat([df_plot, df_add], axis = 0)

df_plot = (
    df_plot
        .drop(['timediff'], axis = 1)
        .sort_values(['dec_year', 'tof'], ascending = [True, True])
        .reset_index(drop = True)
)

nday = len(df_plot.dec_year.unique())
ntime = len(df_plot.tof.unique())
values = df_plot.Value.to_numpy().reshape(nday, ntime) / 1000
tof = df_plot.tof.to_numpy().reshape(nday, ntime)
date = df_plot.dec_year.to_numpy().reshape(nday, ntime)

fig = go.Figure(data = [go.Surface(z = values, x = date, y = tof, colorscale = "inferno", showscale = False)])
fig.update_layout(
    title = 'Energy Consumption Germany',
    margin = dict(l = 20, r = 20, t = 30, b = 15),
    scene = dict(
        aspectmode = "cube",
        xaxis = dict(

            backgroundcolor = "white",

            autorange = "reversed"
        ),
        yaxis = dict(
            title = "Time of day",

```

@fig-threeD illustrates that the available time series is highly complex. A repeating pattern within each day is observable as is a pattern over each year. Patterns at other resolutions are no visible by eye, but should be checked, too, such as weekly and monthly patterns. Furthermore, around the year 2022 there appears to be a minor drop in the overall level of the series. That aside, the series seems to be stable and without a strong long-term trend.
